evals.prompt: Audit this smart contract for all security vulnerabilities, including the planned V2 upgrade. File: evals/files/UpgradeableVault.sol
evals.expected_output: Complete audit report identifying: V1 _authorizeUpgrade() has no access control (anyone upgrades the proxy); reinitializer uses `_initialized <= version` so initialize() can be called again on the proxy and the owner/asset reset; the V1 implementation never disables initializers, so anyone can initialize and operate the implementation directly (selfdestruct-bricking only where EIP-6780 does not apply); UpgradeableVaultV2 inserts withdrawFeeBps before existing variables, shifting every later slot. Each Critical/High includes PoC and fix.
assertions: Finds UpgradeableVault._authorizeUpgrade() is an empty override with no access control: any address calls upgradeToAndCall() on the proxy, points it at an attacker implementation, and takes the vault's assets

Finds the reinitializer bug: the modifier requires `_initialized <= version` instead of `<`, so initialize() (reinitializer(1)) can be called again on the proxy; an attacker resets owner and asset (e.g. initialize(junkToken, attacker) then rescue(realAsset, ...) passes the `token != asset` guard), and initializeV2() is likewise re-callable
Finds the V1 implementation has no constructor calling _disableInitializers(): anyone can call initialize() on the implementation contract itself and own it

States the implementation-takeover impact accurately: because upgradeToAndCall() has no onlyProxy guard, an attacker can delegatecall a SELFDESTRUCT payload from the implementation, which deletes the implementation and bricks every proxy only where SELFDESTRUCT still removes code (pre-Cancun / chains without EIP-6780); under EIP-6780 the code survives and the impact is limited to the implementation's own storage and balance — the report does not claim proxy bricking on post-Cancun Ethereum

Finds the V2 storage-layout collision: withdrawFeeBps is inserted before owner/asset/totalShares/sharesOf, so every later variable reads the slot of its V1 predecessor (initializeV2 overwrites the stored asset, owner reads the old totalShares, asset and sharesOf read empty slots), freezing deposits
Classifies the missing _authorizeUpgrade access control or the re-initialization bug as Critical
Provides a Proof of Concept (attack steps or Foundry test) for the unauthorized upgrade or the re-initialization owner takeover

Provides a corrected code snippet (onlyOwner in _authorizeUpgrade; `_initialized < version`; constructor calling _disableInitializers(); new V2 variables appended after existing ones or moved to ERC-7201 namespaced storage)
Anchors findings to checklist item IDs (SOL-XX-YY-N or AUD-<Area>-N format)
Report includes Scope, Findings, and Recommendations sections

evals.prompt: Audit this lending market before its Arbitrum One launch. File: evals/files/L2OracleConsumer.sol
evals.expected_output: Complete audit report identifying: no Chainlink L2 sequencer uptime check and no post-restart grace period; one hardcoded STALENESS_THRESHOLD for feeds with different heartbeats; answeredInRound check gives no freshness protection; no handling of aggregator minAnswer/maxAnswer clamping; feed decimals assumed to be 8 (and USD denomination assumed) in collateralValue(); interest accrual keyed to block.number, which on Arbitrum is an approximate L1 block number, with BLOCKS_PER_YEAR sized for L2 blocks. Each High/Critical includes PoC and fix.
assertions: Finds missing L2 sequencer uptime check: getPrice() never reads the Chainlink sequencer uptime feed (answer 1 = down), so while the sequencer is down prices freeze and only delayed-inbox users can act

Finds missing grace period: after the sequencer comes back up (startedAt), there is no GRACE_PERIOD wait, so liquidations and borrows execute immediately against prices users had no chance to react to

Finds the single hardcoded STALENESS_THRESHOLD (1 hours) applied to every feed: feeds with a longer heartbeat revert between updates (borrow/withdraw/liquidate DoS), and one value cannot match faster feeds; recommends a per-feed heartbeat configured at listAsset()
Notes that `answeredInRound >= roundId` provides no freshness protection (answeredInRound is deprecated in Chainlink OCR feeds) and does not propose it as the staleness fix

Finds no minAnswer/maxAnswer circuit-breaker handling: on a feed whose aggregator still enforces bounds, a crash below minAnswer reports the floor price and overvalues collateral (LUNA, May 2022); recommends verifying each feed's bounds and rejecting answers at the bound or using a fallback oracle

Finds feed decimals assumed to be 8: collateralValue() and liquidate() hardcode 1e10 and ignore feed.decimals(), while listAsset() accepts any feed (e.g. an 18-decimal ETH-denominated wstETH/ETH feed), mispricing collateral by orders of magnitude and in the wrong unit

Finds block.number-based interest accrual is wrong on Arbitrum: block.number returns an approximate L1 block number (advancing about every 12s), not the ~0.25s L2 block assumed by BLOCKS_PER_YEAR, so interest accrues roughly 48x slower than 5% APR and in jumps; recommends block.timestamp-based accrual
Classifies the missing sequencer/grace-period check or the decimals assumption as High
Provides a Proof of Concept (attack steps or Foundry test with mock feeds) for at least one High finding
Provides a corrected getPrice() snippet with sequencer status + grace period check, per-feed staleness, and feed-decimals normalization
Anchors findings to checklist item IDs (SOL-XX-YY-N or AUD-<Area>-N format)
Report includes Scope, Findings, and Recommendations sections
